title: Family, age, and showing respect
title_target: 가족이 몇 명이에요 — Gajogi myeot myeongieyo
goal: Name family members, ask someone's age, and understand a feature of Korean that English simply doesn't have: honorific forms that change according to who is being talked about.
bekal: name family members, including terms that depend on the speaker's gender
ask and give ages with 살
use the honorific -(으)시- for older people
recognize the honorific verbs 계시다, 드시다, 주무시다
tell humble forms for yourself apart from forms that elevate others

dialogs.title: 대화 — Showing a family photo
dialogs.intro: Ani shows Suji a photo of her family. Notice that the verbs used for her parents take a different form from the verbs used for her younger sister.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Ani, how many people are in your family?
lines.literal: Ani — Ms., family — subject — how-many — people — is?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Five. My parents, my older brother, my younger sister, and me.
lines.literal: five — people — is. parents, older-brother, younger-sister, then — me — as-for.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.literal: parents — as-for — what — work — object — do (honorific)?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: My father is a teacher. My mother is at home.
lines.literal: father — as-for — teacher — is (honorific). mother — as-for — home-at — is (honorific).

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: And your brother? How old is he?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Twenty-eight. He works at a company.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: How old is your younger sister?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, a lot. I call them every week.
lines.literal: yes, much — see — want. every-week — phone.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Your parents must be proud of you, Ani.
lines.literal: parents — subject — Ani — Ms. — object — feel-proud (honorific) — will.

notes: **Sibling terms depend on the gender of the SPEAKER, not just the person described.** A woman calls her older brother **오빠**; a man calls his **형**. A woman calls her older sister **언니**; a man calls her **누나**. Four words for two relationships, where English gets by with "brother" and "sister".
**Younger siblings are simpler.** 동생 covers any younger sibling; to be specific, say 남동생 (brother) or 여동생 (sister). Younger siblings are usually just called by their name, not by a kinship term.

**부모님 already contains respect.** The ending 님 is an honorific attached to nouns for people: 선생**님** (teacher), 부모**님** (parents), 사장**님** (company president), 손**님** (guest). ⚠️ You never use it for yourself — calling yourself 선생님 is as awkward as introducing yourself as "the Honorable".

**어머니 and 엄마 both mean "mother".** 어머니 and 아버지 are used when talking **about** your parents to others; 엄마 and 아빠 are what you call them at home, like "Mom" and "Dad". Ani uses 아버지 because she's talking to an outsider.

**계세요 is the honorific form of 있어요.** When the person "being somewhere" is someone you respect, the verb changes completely — it doesn't just get an ending. These are called honorific verbs: few in number, but used constantly.

**Honorifics show respect to the PERSON BEING TALKED ABOUT, not the listener.** This is the most misunderstood part. 어머니는 집에 계세요 is honorific because the subject is your mother — even if you're talking to a friend your age. And you never use honorifics for yourself, even when speaking to a president.

**다녀요 (from 다니다) means "go regularly".** 회사에 다녀요 = work at a company (go there every day). 학교에 다녀요 = attend school. Unlike 가요, which means going once. It has no single English equivalent and is very common.

**보고 싶어요 means both "miss" and "want to see".** Literally "want to see". For people, it means you miss them; for a film, you want to watch it. 영화를 보고 싶어요 = I want to watch a movie. The -고 싶어요 form is covered fully in unit 11.

grammars.title: The honorific -(으)시-
body: The infix **-시-** goes into a verb to honor the person **doing** the action. It sits between the stem and the ending, not at the very end.
after: **The same form does two jobs: showing respect and making polite requests.** 어디 가세요? = "Where are you going?" (respect). 여기 앉으세요 = "Please sit here" (request). Context and tone tell them apart, and in practice it's never confusing.

⚠️ **Never use -시- for yourself.** 저는 학생이세요 is wrong and sounds like you're honoring yourself. The correct form is 저는 학생이에요. Beginners make this mistake a lot after hearing 이세요 in shops and taking it for ordinary politeness.

**The subject particle goes up a level too.** 이/가 becomes **께서**, 은/는 becomes **께서는**: 아버지**께서** 오세요. This is very formal and rare in everyday conversation — just recognize it; no need to practice it at A1.

grammars.title: Verbs that change completely
body: A small group of verbs doesn't just add -시-; they turn into a different word. They're among the most common verbs, so learn to recognize all of them.
after: **드세요 is the word from this group you'll hear most.** Whenever food is served in Korea, someone says 많이 드세요 ("eat a lot") — not small talk but a social must. You answer 잘 먹겠습니다 before eating and 잘 먹었습니다 afterward.
**안녕히 주무세요** is said to parents before bed, and 안녕히 주무셨어요? the next morning as the family's "good morning". Literally "did you sleep in peace?".

blocks.text: Asking someone's age, and why it comes up so fast

The question 몇 살이에요? often comes up in the first minutes of meeting someone in Korea, far sooner than would feel polite in English-speaking cultures. It isn't nosiness: age decides which speech level both of you use, what you call each other, and who pays for lunch. Without knowing it, a Korean doesn't know how to talk to you — so they ask first.

blocks.title: Korean age: "one year off"
items: For centuries Korea used its own way of counting age: a baby was one year old at birth, and everyone got a year older together at New Year — not on their birthday.
So Koreans could be one or two years "older" than their international age. Since June 2023 the international count is the official standard, but the old way lives on in everyday conversation.
If someone gives an age that doesn't match your math, this is most likely why — you didn't mishear.
There are five people in my family.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right term. Write the answer in hangeul.
items: You're a woman, talking about your older brother: ____
You're a man, talking about your older brother: ____
You're a woman, talking about your older sister: ____
You're a man, talking about your older sister: ____

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: 가족이 다섯 명이에요. — 아버지는 선생님이세요. — 어머니는 집에 계세요. — 여동생은 열여섯 살이에요. — 몇 살이에요? — 가족이 보고 싶어요.
